description: Lahore Grammar School Defence's O1 26-27 Batch
summary:
The Forgotten Explorers is an interactive website that tells the stories of the machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars. Users scroll a timeline of landings from 1966 to 2021 while a globe turns to each site, then open any of ten missions, from Apollo 11’s Eagle to the Ingenuity helicopter. Each mission page states how the mission ended, shows its story , and finishes with a short fun quiz with hints and badges.

The site then lets users experience the missions. They can take a 3D spacecraft apart, fly a landing, walk around the landing site as an astronaut to find what was left behind, and drive the Opportunity rover from its landing to the 2018 dust storm that ended it. A live page shows which spacecraft are talking to Earth right now.

It addresses the challenge by turning “abandoned” hardware into characters people care about, and by showing that some of it still works e.g reflectors left by Apollo crews are still used today.
details:
What it does. The Forgotten Explorers is a website about the equipment NASA left on the Moon and Mars. It has four parts:

Read. A scrolling home page with a timeline of 17 landings, and ten mission pages (Apollo 11, 15 and 17, Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity). Each page shows whether the mission succeeded, when and why it ended, a first-person story, a timeline, why it mattered, and its NASA sources. Long text stays behind “Read more” buttons.
Test yourself. A fun quiz per mission with hints, stars and badges.
Experience. 3D spacecraft that come apart to show their components ,Moon and Mars globes with real landing sites; a landing game with controls and autopilot; on foot exploration with objects to find and inspect; and “Live the life of Opportunity”, where the player drives the rover, photographs discoveries and sends them to Earth.
Live. A page showing which spacecraft NASA’s Deep Space Network is in contact with, where NASA’s active spacecraft are, and NASA’s newest images.

A guided tour introduces the features one at a time on a first visit, and a small help bot answers questions from a checked list of facts.

Benefits and intended impact. The project is aimed at students and the general public. It replaces the idea of “space junk” with stories: why each machine was sent, what it found, and why it was left. It also teaches that some left-behind equipment is still doing science.

Tools. JavaScript, HTML and CSS. React, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei for 3D, Rapier for physics, GSAP for animation, Vite to build, and the Web Audio API for all sound and music.

Creativity. The stories are told by the machines themselves. The surface worlds curve and wrap so a player can walk all the way around. The games can be shown in a “television broadcast” style, labelled as a simulation.

What we considered. Accuracy: facts come from NASA mission pages listed on each page, creative writing is labelled as such, and imagined elements (the jetpack, walking on Mars, compressed distances) are stated on the site. Overload: short pages, a guided tour, and no right-click menus interrupting the games. Honesty about AI: the site states where AI tools were used.
